question.text: If the Thomson model of the atom was correct, then the result of Rutherford's gold foil experiment would have been:

options.text: All of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">α</mi></math>-particles pass through the gold foil without decrease in speed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">α</mi></math>-particles are deflected over a wide range of angles.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">α</mi></math>-particles pass through the gold foil deflected by small angles and with reduced speed.

solution.text: According to Thomson's plum pudding model, protons are diffused in a positively charged cloud (charge is not centred) and the negatively charged particles are embedded in it. So, the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">α</mi></math>- particles would deviate by small angles and due to repulsion from protons, their speed would decrease.
